1.24

F. Pronouns and gender

Every noun in German is assigned a grammatical gender (der | die | das), and these gender distinctions apply as well to the corresponding pronouns (er | sie | es).


F.1

English speakers intuitively make the connection between natural gender and these pronouns:

Der Student? → Er ist …

The (male) student? He is …

Die Professorin? → Sie ist …

The (female) professor? She is …

But German makes this connection for inanimate objects as well, using er | sie | es to stand in for masculine, feminine and neuter nouns, where English simply uses it:

Der Film? → Er ist …

The film? It is …

Die Aufgabe? → Sie ist …

The assignment? It is …

Das Buch? → Es ist …

The book? It is …

Since plural nouns show no gender distinctions, there is only one pronoun for they: sie

die Studenten

the students

die Städte

the cities

die Filme

the films

die Bücher

the books

→ und sie sind …

and they are …

There is considerable debate in Germany, Austria and Switzerland surrounding the use of gendered pronouns and masculine plural forms meant to refer to everyone (e.g., Studenten in the list above). If you're interested, you can find a short introductory NPR article here — and your instructor can point you to more resources.

content:
F.2

Some languages (such as Spanish) delete subject pronouns once the subject has been established, rather than repeating it in subsequent clauses or sentences. But in most cases, German requires a subject — either a pronoun or a noun — in every clause or sentence.

Der Mann heißt Alexander.

The man’s name is Alexander.

Er ist 30 Jahre alt.

He’s 30 years old.

Er wohnt in Berlin.

He lives in Berlin.

Er spielt Fußball jeden Sonntag.

He plays soccer every Sunday.

That said, it’s certainly possible for a subject to be connected with more than one verb in an extended clause: Er ist 30 Jahre alt, wohnt in Berlin und spielt Fußball. But if the information is divided into separate clauses or sentences, each usually has a noun or pronoun subject.

G. Subjects + Verbs: wir / ihr / Sie

wir we

ihr you (all) [familiar]

Sie you (all) [formal]


G.1

Below are the verb forms of sein and haben that you use when talking about a group that includes you (wir); when addressing a group of people with whom you use the familiar form for you (ihr); and when addressing a group of people with whom you use the formal form for you (Sie):


sein

haben

wir we

sind

haben

ihr you (all)

[familiar]

seid

habt

Sie you (all)

[formal]

sind

haben


NB: Sie is the formal form for you when addressing either one person or several people, and the verb endings are identical for both situations. This means that only the context — not the grammatical form — can tell you if Sie is plural or singular in a given sentence.


G.1
label: G.1

content:
G.2.

For most other verbs, the forms used with wir, ihr and Sie are highly predictable — just the stem plus the appropriate ending. (Notice that the endings are identical for wir and Sie .)


spiel- find-
wir [stem] + en spielen finden
ihr [stem] + t spielt findet
Sie [stem] + en spielen finden

As you’ve learned for other forms, when the verb stem ends with -d or -t, an -e- is inserted before the -t:

Wie findet ihr das Essen hier? What do you (all) think of the food here?

Ihr arbeitet zu viel! You (all) work too much!

H. I like ... / like to ...

To express an opinion, it's helpful to know how to say I like that or I like doing that. Here are several options for doing so; you’ll learn more in the chapters to come.


H.1

To say you like (or don’t like) something or someone, as represented by a noun or a pronoun, you can use these expressions:

Ich finde [X] + [Adjektiv].

  • Ich finde den Film »Dumm und Dümmer« fantastisch!

  • Spinnst du?° Ich finde »Dumm und Dümmer« nur dumm.


[X] gefällt mir. [literally: ... is pleasing to me.]

  • Der Film gefällt mir.


[X] gefällt mir nicht. [literally: ... is not pleasing to me.]

  • Was? Also, er gefällt mir gar nicht.


If [X] is plural, the verb takes the plural form gefallen: Meine Kurse gefallen mir!

H.1
label: H.1

content:
H.2

To express the idea of liking to do something, e.g., I like to play the piano, German uses the adverb gern [literally: gladly] after the verb. You’ll learn more about this later, but you can form simple sentences with it now:


arbeiten gern

schreiben gern

sein gern

gehen gern

Ich arbeite gern.

Schreibst du gern?

Er ist gern zu Hause.

Wir gehen gern in die Stadt.

I like to work.

Do you like to write?

He likes to be at home.

We like to go into the city.

To say you don’t like doing something, use nicht gern. (You can intensify the phrase by adding gar: Ich mache diese Aufgaben gar nicht gern!)


arbeiten nicht gern

schreiben nicht gern

sein nicht gern

gehen nicht gern

Ich arbeite gar nicht gern.

Schreibst du nicht gern?

Er ist nicht gern zu Hause.

Wir gehen nicht gern in die Stadt.

I really don’t like to work.

Don’t you like to write?

He doesn’t like to be at home.

We don’t like to go into the city.
